newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE builders to feel pinch from labour expulsion.
newsitem.headline: UAE builders to feel pinch from labour expulsion.

text.p: The exodus of low-wage manual and semi-skilled labourers from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has impacted construction projects in the oil-rich Gulf state, managers at building firms in the UAE said on Monday.

The UAE's decision to expel illegal expatriate workers, who come mostly from the Indian subcontinent and Asia, had left some construction firms, in particular subcontractors, stripped of their work force forcing them to suspend building work.

"Our subcontracted labour has left the country. The work will be delayed for the time being," said a manager at a local contractor close to completing a block of residential villas in the UAE capital Abu Dhabi.
"There must be a dialogue with the Ministry of Labour and work out a successful solution," he added.
Diplomats expect up to 200,000 expatriates will leave the UAE when a government amnesty for foreign workers without proper residency or work permits expires at the end of September.
The UAE has said that the number of illegal workers -- those who have over stayed their original work documents or smuggled themselves into the state -- posed a threat to UAE security.

Subcontractors rely heavily on imported labour from India, Bangladesh and Pakistan to erect the houses, roads, office blocks and public work projects that have turned the UAE into one of the leading and developed economies of the Gulf.

Subcontractors, typically employing between 50 to 100 workers, say they have had to release staff, that projects could be delayed and some voiced fears that they would face financial penalties if construction projects overran.
They also fear inflation, currently held in check at six percent, could be undermined if labour costs rose and that businesses faced disruption.

Ibrahim Suleiman, a managing partner at Suweidi Engineering in Abu Dhabi, estimated construction workers wages would rise between 10 and 20 percent because companies facing project deadlines would pay higher salaries, the UAE Arabic daily Al-Khaleej newspaper reported on Monday.

A typical salary for a construction worker ranged between 400 and 800 UAE dirhams a month ($108-$217), a wage level that made creating cities in the desert viable and helped foster a $6 billion construction sector.
Industry sources say it was common for labourers who had no immigration paper work to find jobs in construction.
"There was a runaway labour force...a black market to achieve economic goals," one manager at a building firm said.
Expatriate workers make up 75 percent of the UAE's 2.4 million population.

They have formed the backbone of the Gulf Arab state's economic development since petrodollars flooded the Gulf in the early 1970s and provide the labour to meet the UAE construction boom that followed the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

Major international and Gulf firms based in the UAE largely welcomed the amnesty law and down played the effects tighter UAE labour laws would have on their operations, pointing out that they had been observing labour laws all along.

Few of these firms, employing thousands rather than hundreds of expatriate workers, discounted the possibility that a smaller labour pool would fan workers' salaries higher with a resulting inflationary pressures.

"It will create a more level playing field. I cannot see any major problem for legitimate businesses...I see no effect," another construction executive said, adding that the labour ministry was able to meet any request from firms for staff.
The government's decision to allow blue-collar workers to change company sponsors and remain in the country was also welcomed by UAE-based firms.
